solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: A posh roll? (8,7)

blocks.note: the surface reads this as upmarket; the setter means belonging to the aristocracy
the surface wants a bread roll; the setter means a roll-call, a register of names

annotation.surface: Someone orders an upmarket bread bun.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: 'roll' looks like bread, but it is a list. Debrett's Peerage is the British reference book of the nobility and their families.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic definition: the book is a register whose every entry is titled, so it is a roll of the posh.

entries.clue: Ties up footwear first son swapped with daughter (5)

indicators.note: to swap is to exchange, so the son's letter goes out and the daughter's comes into the same slot

blocks.note: socks are worn on the feet
s = son, here the first letter of SOCKS

annotation.surface: Someone does up their shoes, with a family squabble over whose turn it is.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ties up' reads as lacing shoes, but it is what a boat does at a quay.
annotation.definitionFit: A nautical sense: mooring a vessel at a quay is tying it up.

entries.clue: Rascals touring church half-cut left in cuffs (9)

indicators.note: to tour a place is to go all around it, so BRATS goes around the rest
cut down to half, so only half of LEFT is kept

annotation.surface: Drunken young troublemakers on a church tour end up in handcuffs.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' is British slang for drunk, which fits the rascals, but here it trims a word to half its length. BRA(CE LE)TS.
annotation.definitionFit: Old criminal slang: handcuffs worn on the wrists were called by the jewellery's name.

entries.clue: Advantage of leaving the lid off of jam (4)

indicators.note: a lid is the top, and a down answer's top is its first letter

blocks.note: to wedge a door is to jam it

annotation.surface: Opening a jar of preserve without a lid on has its benefits.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Jam' looks like fruit preserve with a lid; it is a verb, to wedge fast.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as in having a slight lead over a rival.

entries.clue: Coach drinks beers regularly in ground (7)

indicators.note: a drinker takes the drink inside, so TRAIN holds the other letters
at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken

blocks.note: the second and fourth letters of bEeRs

annotation.surface: A sports coach knocks back beers every so often down at the ground.
annotation.walkthrough: The coach sits in the ground's bar in the surface; in the wordplay 'Coach' is a verb, and 'drinks' is what swallows the beer letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a stretch of land, judged by its physical features.

entries.clue: Shady type in jumper individual cut short (7)

indicators.note: something cut short loses its end, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: a para is a paratrooper, who jumps from planes

annotation.surface: A shifty character hides among the paratroopers, or wears a sweater.
annotation.walkthrough: A 'shady type' sounds like a crook, but here it is a thing that makes shade. 'Jumper' tempts as a sweater, the everyday British word for a pullover.
annotation.definitionFit: A witty definition: a sunshade is literally a type of thing that gives shade.

entries.clue: Conservative involved in passing soldiers amphetamines? (9)

indicators.note: to be involved in something is to be inside it

blocks.note: soldier ants, the crossword's usual worker insects

annotation.surface: A Tory politician is caught up with troops who are taking speed.
annotation.walkthrough: EX(C)IT + ANTS. The question mark admits that amphetamines are just one example.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: amphetamines are one kind of stimulant drug.

entries.clue: A wicked back on the ball (5)

indicators.note: going back means reading from the end to the start

annotation.surface: A footballer's fierce fullback has the ball at his feet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Back' and 'ball' paint a football pitch, so 'back' looks like a defender; it is only a direction.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: being quick-witted and alert to something.

entries.clue: Has opener ruined cans? (9)

indicators.note: something ruined is wrecked, and its letters are rebuilt in a new order

annotation.surface: Someone asks whether the tin opener has wrecked the cans.
annotation.walkthrough: The tin opener makes 'cans' look like tins; it is slang for headphones.
annotation.definitionFit: Slang: cans are headphones, worn over the ears.

entries.clue: Cold rage coming after large mistake (7)

indicators.note: what comes after follows, so ANGER is placed after L

blocks.note: C = cold, as on a tap

annotation.surface: Cold fury follows a big blunder.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is British slang for a glaring blunder, as in 'drop a clanger'.
annotation.definitionFit: British slang for an embarrassing blunder, one that makes a loud noise.

entries.clue: Swing that’s rusted at front’s more unstable (7)

indicators.note: what sits at the front of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: to swing to and fro is to rock

annotation.surface: A garden swing with rusty front legs is getting wobblier.
annotation.walkthrough: 'That's' has to be expanded to 'that is' before it becomes the Latin abbreviation.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: rocky means shaky, and this is its comparative.

entries.clue: Worrying situation if wife leaves for month in spring (4)

indicators.note: to leave something for another is to give up one for the other, so W departs and M takes its place

blocks.note: to be in a stew is to be in a state of worry

annotation.surface: A husband frets that his wife will leave him for a month in the spring.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spring' looks like the season beside 'month', but it is a verb: to spring from something is to arise from it.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: problems that arise from a cause spring from it.

entries.clue: Choppers manufactured as the fleet needs transportation (5,5)

indicators.note: transported letters are carried off and set down elsewhere, in a new order

annotation.surface: Helicopters are built because the navy needs a way to move people.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Choppers' suggests helicopters in a naval surface; it is slang for teeth, and 'manufactured' makes them artificial.
annotation.definitionFit: Slang plus a qualifier: choppers are teeth, and made ones are dentures.

entries.clue: Ultimately corrupt motive for crime (7)

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so the word's end letter is taken

annotation.surface: A detective concludes that a corrupt motive lay behind an offence.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a detective's verdict, so 'motive for crime' reads as one phrase; it splits after 'motive'.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: betraying one's country is one particular offence.

entries.clue: US and Chile put out after British invasion! (3,6)

indicators.note: letters that are out are out of order
an invader gets inside, so B goes in among the rearranged letters

blocks.note: B = British, added among the rearranged letters

annotation.surface: America and Chile are ousted after a British military invasion.
annotation.walkthrough: 'US' is printed as the country, but read it as the pronoun: us, the people at large.
annotation.definitionFit: A pronoun read as a noun: us, ordinary people collectively.

entries.clue: Royals are toppled in revolutionary period (5,4)

indicators.note: knocked over, so the letters fall into a new order

annotation.surface: A monarchy is overthrown during an uprising.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary period' reads as a time of uprising, but it is one full orbit of the Earth.
annotation.definitionFit: A witty definition: the time the Earth takes to revolve once around the Sun.

entries.clue: One illuminating bit of report Network 10 screens (7)

indicators.note: a bit of report is the smallest piece, its first letter
to screen is to shield from view, so TEN hides R inside

blocks.note: the first letter of report, placed inside TEN

annotation.surface: A news item on the Australian TV channel Network 10 sheds light on a story.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Network 10' looks like one name, an Australian TV channel; the two words work separately.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a portable lamp is one thing that gives light.

entries.clue: Cycles taken out of housing development (9)

indicators.note: a housing is the outer casing, so the word's first and last letters are removed

blocks.note: a cycle is one revolution of a wheel
the outer letters R and S are removed

annotation.surface: Bicycles are removed from a new housing estate.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Housing development' reads as one phrase, a new estate, but it splits: 'housing' is the word's outer casing and 'development' is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: gradual change and growth over time.

entries.clue: Greek character in record store close to town (7)

indicators.note: the close of a word is where it ends, its last letter

blocks.note: an EP is an extended-play record

annotation.surface: A Greek person is spotted in a record shop near the town centre.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Record store' reads as a music shop, but it splits into two separate pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: A letter of the alphabet: the fifth one in Greek.

entries.clue: Books an allegedly violent youth after Norway scored? (7)

indicators.note: what comes after follows, so the other pieces follow N

blocks.note: N is Norway's international vehicle code
OT = Old Testament, a set of books
a Teddy boy was a 1950s British youth with a reputation for fights

annotation.surface: A thuggish young man is booked after Norway score a goal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Scored' looks like football beside Norway; a score is written music, so scored means written in musical notation.
annotation.definitionFit: A musical sense: to score a piece is to write it out in notation.

entries.clue: Cloth suits one found in British haberdashers? (7)

indicators.note: something found in a place is inside it, so I sits within the other letters

blocks.note: haberdashers are shops selling sewing goods, the question mark admitting they are only one kind

annotation.surface: A tailored suit is found in a British draper's shop.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The cloth' means the clergy, and 'suits' is slang for the people in charge, so cloth suits are senior churchmen.
annotation.definitionFit: Two slang senses combined: the cloth is the clergy and suits are the bosses.

entries.clue: Shoes villain gets in black (small-sized) (7)

indicators.note: to get in is to enter, so ROGUE goes inside the B and S

blocks.note: S = small, as on clothing labels

annotation.surface: A villain buys a small pair of black shoes.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is a sturdy leather shoe with decorative punched holes, originally Irish and Scottish.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: one style of leather shoe.

entries.clue: Don’t use rod criminal grasped (10)

indicators.note: a criminal is crooked, and crooked letters are bent out of order

annotation.surface: A warning not to use a rod, which a crook has seized.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Grasped' pretends a criminal grabbed the rod; it means taken in mentally.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative synonym: grasping an idea is taking it in mentally.

entries.clue: Speak slowly and at length and inspire learner (5)

blocks.note: to inspire is to breathe in, to draw breath
L = learner, the L-plate on a British learner's car

annotation.surface: A teacher talks slowly and at length to inspire a student.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Inspire' reads as motivate, but its literal Latin sense is to breathe in.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: talking with vowels stretched out lazily.

entries.clue: Heroin is rubbish (4)

blocks.note: the drug, known by a street name

annotation.surface: A blunt verdict on the drug.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is an anti-drug slogan; both halves define the same four-letter word, and 'junkie' comes from the drug sense.
annotation.definitionFit: Street slang for the drug, and an everyday word for worthless clutter.

entries.clue: Sorts issue after drinking last of gin (5)

indicators.note: a drinker takes the drink inside, so KIDS takes the letter in
the last of anything is its end, so the final letter

blocks.note: the final letter of gin, placed inside KIDS

annotation.surface: Some sort of trouble follows after the gin is finished.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Issue' looks like a problem arising, but it means children. KI(N)DS.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: types or varieties.

entries.clue: Mark essays carefully, but just one section (4)

indicators.note: only a section of the words is used, so the answer lies inside them

annotation.surface: A teacher marks essays with care, but only one part of them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mark' reads as grading homework, but it is the definition, a noun.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a blemish left on the skin after a wound heals.

entries.clue: Most unproductive field next to den (7)

indicators.note: things next to each other sit side by side, so the pieces join

blocks.note: a lea is a meadow, a poetic word crosswords love
a den and a nest are both lairs

annotation.surface: The poorest farmland lies beside an animal's lair.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface wants 'most unproductive field' as one phrase about poor farmland; 'field' belongs to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A superlative sense: lean years or harvests yield little.

entries.clue: Fellow leaving social event affected charm (7)

indicators.note: one who is leaving goes out, so F departs from the word

blocks.note: a function is a formal party

annotation.surface: A man leaves a party, put off by someone's fake charm.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is the oily, ingratiating manner behind the adjective unctuous.
annotation.definitionFit: A less common sense: a smooth, insincere manner that is put on.

entries.clue: Distribute poor grass in cold city abroad (8,7)

indicators.note: to distribute is to spread around, so the letters are scattered into a new order

annotation.surface: An instruction to spread feeble grass seed in cold weather.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is gardening advice; the answer is in the USA, 'abroad' to the British setter.
annotation.definitionFit: A vague definition by place: a US city in the Rockies, foreign to a British solver.
